extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, scholars, and literary critics (men of letters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for study, conversation, writing, and the criticism of poetry (especially pastoral poetry). Includes standards for readability, originality, propriety of subject-matter, and the balance of learning and social skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading, conversation, and writing balance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Reading makes a full man, conversation a ready man, and writing an exact man."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate all three: read to accumulate knowledge, converse to gain facility in expression and adaptability, and write to fix thoughts and achieve method and exactness. Excess in any one without the others produces imbalance (e.g., a recluse loses elocution; mere conversers gain facility but not method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult predecessors / value of libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and students should not disdain libraries or assert they can learn nothing from predecessors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult celebrated authors' works to comprehend their systems and reasonings; learning from former generations strengthens one's performance. Declaring one can learn nothing from predecessors is arrogance and weakens one's claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make writing and speech appropriate to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid presupposing readers possess advanced degrees of skill; do not use short hints and obscure allusions that require familiarity only the author has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain terms and concepts clearly (example: a lecturer failing to explain 'opacum' and 'pellucidum' to his audience). Tailor complexity to expected reader/listener competence to avoid obscurity and incomprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test and defend opinions through conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Solitary study tends to let one adopt opinions without sufficient proof; conversation exposes ideas to objections and forces justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discussion to discover weaknesses in favored positions; frequent encounters with differing minds help prepare replies and strengthen reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in presenting arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Only long habit and frequent experiments can confer the power of changing a position into various forms, presenting it in different points of view, connecting it with known truths, and illustrating it by apt similitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn to recast ideas into different forms and to fortify them with intelligible arguments and apt analogies so they survive varied objections and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method and organization in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Method is the excellence of writing, and unconstraint the grace of conversation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use writing to contract and organize thoughts; strive for order, distinction, and precise arrangement. Favor writing for thorough examination and to detect sophisms acquired through loose conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sophistry and dishonest argument in conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Heated talk and eagerness for victory lead some to take advantage of opponents' mistakes and urge proofs that they know have no force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not satisfy oneself with arguments that merely silence others; maintain severity of reason and avoid pursuing winning over truth. Be wary that conversational facility can produce inaccuracy and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep accuracy over copiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Copiousness and facility may be made less valuable by inaccuracy and confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer careful, methodical writing to merely fluent but unexamined discourse; use writing to revise and expose fallacies introduced by conversational habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candour and balanced praise in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should show a spirit of candour and love of truth, remote from bigotry and captiousness; distribute praise justly among ancients and moderns, with sober deference to established reputation and willingness to favor later performances without puerile fondness for novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should avoid blind adoration of antiquity and also avoid indiscriminate praise of novelty; evaluate works on merit with impartiality and measured respect for tradition and innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / inventive power
rubrics_metrics.description: When surveying a genre (e.g., pastorals), consider whether the author can claim praise as an inventor or merely as a successful imitator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work brings new design or truly original elements, or whether it largely copies prior models (example: Virgil copying Theocritus). Original inventive power is prized; mere faithful imitation diminishes inventive credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity appropriate to the pastoral character
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastoral poetry should preserve simplicity; excessive magnificence of diction or elevated sentiment may deviate from the pastoral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether elevated language and splendour suit the pastoral mode or instead undermine its natural simplicity. Deviation from the pastoral character to achieve grandeur can be a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affecting sentiment and pleasing description
rubrics_metrics.description: A pastoral should contain affecting sentiment or pleasing description that strikes the imagination and awakens the passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poems for passages that genuinely move readers (affecting sentiment) and offer pleasing, imaginative description; the absence of such passages weakens the poem's claim to excellence (example: the second pastoral is criticized for lacking such qualities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety and dignity of subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements inconsistent with the genre's dignity (e.g., invectives in pastoral verse) detract from its appropriateness; pastoral innocence should be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid introducing content (such as coarse invective or inappropriate quarrel) that degrades the expected tone and moral character of the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion between performance and occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: The style and grandeur of a poem should be proportioned to the occasion that produced it; disproportion suggests injudicious choice or misapplied effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question whether elevated language and heroic or philosophic strain are warranted by the poem's ostensible purpose (example: a poem that celebrates a private birth but uses heroic diction is disproportionate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mythological imagery vs natural sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive reliance on mythological images (easily invented) may supplant natural, rational sentiment and affect the poem's genuineness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer images and sentiments that feel naturally arising from the pastoral situation rather than contrived mythological ornamentation that can feel manufactured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repeating the same plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of the same plan across multiple pieces (e.g., two contests of shepherds) reflects a reproach to inventive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek variety of design and avoid composing multiple works on too-similar plots or structures; originality includes variety of plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish translation from original composition
rubrics_metrics.description: If much of a piece is merely translation, the author has less claim to originality and should be judged accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how much of the work is genuinely the author's invention versus rendering of others' texts (example: the eighth pastoral is characterized as largely a translation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discernible design and tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem should have a clear design or tendency; works that seem to be merely filler with no obvious purpose are open to reproach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge for unity of purpose and coherent thematic direction; absence of discernible design (example: the ninth pastoral) weakens the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and diversified depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Superior pastoral poetry combines naturalness with variety and diversified images (example: the first pastoral is praised as 'equally natural and more diversified').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value poems that feel authentic to pastoral life and provide varied, vivid scenes and emotions rather than monotony or artifice.
